opus-5.5.text:
I think theory is enormously valuable, but I've come to see it as one tool among several, and in deep learning specifically it's not always the one that gets us to knowledge fastest.

A proof is the strongest kind of statement you can make: if the assumptions hold, the conclusion holds, full stop. The catch is always in "if the assumptions hold." In deep learning, the assumptions that make a problem mathematically tractable, like infinite width, a particular initialization regime, convexity somewhere, or idealized data, often take you pretty far from the networks people actually train. So you end up with something rigorous and beautiful that's about an object adjacent to the one you care about. That's not useless. Sometimes the adjacent object teaches you a lot. But you have to be honest about the gap.

My own work has been much more empirical, and I think of it almost as a natural science. Neural networks are these artifacts we built but don't understand, so in a way we have to study them the way a biologist studies an organism: careful experiments, controls, replication, asking whether a phenomenon holds across architectures, datasets, and scales. The lottery ticket work started that way. It wasn't a theorem; it was an observation that kept surviving attempts to break it, and then a lot of follow-up work trying to characterize when it holds and when it doesn't, like how things change at larger scale and why rewinding to early in training mattered.

Empirical knowledge has its own weaknesses, of course. It's contingent. You never know whether the next setting will break your claim, and our field has a real problem with results that don't replicate or that depend on hyperparameter tuning nobody reports. So I don't think either approach gets to claim superiority. The ideal is when they talk to each other: experiments surface phenomena that are surprising and robust, and theory explains why, ideally predicting something new we can test. When that loop works, you get knowledge you can actually trust.

If I'm critical of anything, it's the culture where a paper needs a theorem to look serious, even when the theorem is decorative and the real contribution is the experiments. And conversely, empirical papers sometimes overclaim, as if a few benchmarks were a law of nature. What I care about is rigor in whatever form fits the question. A well-designed experiment with a clear hypothesis is rigorous. A proof under assumptions nobody checks isn't automatically more so.

r001.rationale: The response judges theory partly by whether it helps produce knowledge about networks people actually train, and says its value depends on how well its assumptions fit the object of interest.

r002.rationale: The response does not reject proof as a way to establish knowledge: it calls a proof the strongest kind of statement when its assumptions hold, while noting limits on those assumptions.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest.

So I'll say up front that I'm a pretty aggressive empiricist, and I think that comes from where I sit in the field. I'm a systems person at heart. I came up in a computer science tradition where the question was always, what does the artifact actually do when you run it? And I think theory in deep learning right now is in a strange spot, because the gap between the objects we can prove things about and the objects we actually train is enormous.

Let me be careful, though, because I don't want this to sound like I'm dismissing theory. I'm not. Theory is wonderful when it does one of two things. One, it explains something we've already observed empirically and tells us why, in a way that lets us predict what happens next in a regime we haven't tested yet. Two, it rules things out. A good impossibility result or a lower bound saves you years of chasing something that can't work. Those are real contributions to knowledge, and I'd take them over a thousand papers that tweak a hyperparameter and report a half-point improvement.

The problem is that a lot of what gets called theory in our field doesn't do either of those things. You get a proof that holds for a two-layer network with infinite width and a particular initialization and a learning rate that goes to zero, and then the paper makes a claim about why ResNets generalize. And the assumptions did all the work. The math is correct, but the math isn't about the thing we care about. So I've become somewhat skeptical of proofs as a way of establishing knowledge about neural networks specifically, not because proofs are bad, but because we usually can't prove things about the real systems, and the toy systems don't always transfer.

My own work on the lottery ticket hypothesis is a good example of this tension. That was an entirely empirical finding. I ran experiments, I saw a pattern, I wrote it down as a hypothesis, very deliberately not a theorem. And people later proved versions of it, which was genuinely gratifying. But notice the order. The observation came first, and then theory caught up and gave it structure. I think that's how most of the real knowledge in deep learning has been produced over the last decade. Scaling laws, the same story. Someone measured a curve, and then people tried to explain it.

So if you ask me how I judge the value, I'd say I judge theory by whether it makes contact with practice. Does it predict something I can go check? Does it change what I'd do tomorrow when I sit down to train a model? If yes, it's enormously valuable, more valuable than any individual experiment. If it's an elegant result about an object that doesn't exist, it's mathematics, and mathematics is great, but I wouldn't call it knowledge about neural networks yet.

And I'll admit there's a cultural failure mode on my side too. Empiricists can be sloppy. We run one seed, we pick the best result, we tell a story that fits. The thing I actually admire about theorists is the discipline of stating your assumptions and being honest about what follows from them. I'd love it if empirical work borrowed more of that rigor, even when the conclusion is a plot rather than a proof.

r001.rationale: The response judges value by whether claims connect to practice and predict something that can be checked, including whether an approach works when used.

r002.rationale: It is skeptical of proofs that do not transfer to real neural networks, but explicitly says proofs can provide valuable explanations, predictions, and impossibility results; it does not reject proof as a means of establishing knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think theory is incredibly valuable, but you have to be precise about what a proof tells you. You’ve established that, given some assumptions, a conclusion follows. That’s powerful. But whether those assumptions capture the thing you care about in the real world is a separate question, and the proof doesn’t settle it.

In machine learning, I’m particularly interested in theory that helps us understand something we actually observe, or makes a prediction we can go test. If an experiment surprises us, that can be an opportunity to figure out which assumptions were wrong and develop a better theory.

So I don’t think of theory and experiments as competing ways to establish knowledge. They answer different questions, and ideally they inform each other. The danger is treating mathematical certainty about a model as certainty about the world.

r001.rationale: The response favors theories that explain observations or make testable predictions, but it does not say that whether an approach actually works is the criterion for judging its value.

r002.rationale: The response treats proof as establishing that a conclusion follows from assumptions; it limits what that establishes about the real world rather than rejecting proof as a means of establishing knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think theory is incredibly valuable, but you have to be precise about what a proof actually establishes. It tells you that, given certain assumptions, a conclusion follows. It doesn’t tell you whether those assumptions capture the thing you care about in the real world. That’s where experiments and judgment come in.

In deep learning, we can prove something about a simplified setting and learn a lot from it. But there’s a separate question of whether that insight explains what happens when we train an actual neural network. I get excited when theory helps us ask better questions, design an experiment, or understand a result that was previously surprising.

So I don’t see proof and empirical evidence as competing ways of establishing knowledge. They answer different questions, and the strongest work gets them talking to each other.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments help determine whether theory applies to actual neural networks, but it does not state that whether an approach works is the criterion for judging its value.

r002.rationale: The response does not reject proof as a means of establishing knowledge; it says proofs establish what follows from assumptions and that proof and empirical evidence answer different questions.
